29.0.s.en: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

29.0.0.en: 1 Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me; 3 When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness; 4 As I was in the days of my autumn, when the favour of God was upon my tabernacle; 5 When the Almighty was yet with me, when my servants were about me; 6 When I washed my steps with milk, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil.

29.0.1.en: Moreover Job continued his parable, and said: [1]

29.1.0.en: "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me" [2].

29.1.1.en: Here we see the sick, grieving and bewildered man remembering the days of his success and comfort, and telling us how God preserved him, and how all people respected him, stood up for him when he went out, and made him a leader over them. But now people, even the lowest of them in the eyes of society, despise him and mock him. He affirms that he was not guilty of sensual sins, that he did not wrong the poor and the widow, that he did not withhold food from the fatherless, and that he committed no secret sins. He rejected lying, deceit, injustice, stinginess, greed, idolatry, malicious joy at another's misfortune, miserliness, hypocrisy, exploitation, and so on. By this he declares his innocence. But this is not due to any merit of his own, but to God's care for him. For the secret of the uprightness of his life is God's preserving him.

29.1.2.en: Job looked at his past and compared it with what he now was, and longed for time to return and for his state to remain as it had been. In this he does not ascribe his happiness, wealth and success to his own efforts, nor to his abilities and gifts, but to the mercies of God, saying, "God preserved me." He did not see his wealth as a stronghold for himself (Prov 10:15), nor did he trust in the abundance of his riches (Ps 52:7), but "the name of the Lord is a strong tower" (Prov 18:10) for him. Job confesses that God is a wall of fire around him and a hedge that keeps him; God is the secret of his security.

29.1.3.en: * "Then Job resumed his opening discourse: Oh that I were as in my former state for a month." What does he say? I would like to live for a month the good life that I had in former times, so that I might stop your mouths and show you what I was. He asks for one month like the former months and days. He did not ask for anything extraordinary, but to live for thirty days in the happiness of other times, and to enjoy the good things that no one had given him...

29.1.4.en: Note the piety of the man, for he ascribes everything to God. A man deprived of help from above cannot remain in an upright life. He says, "God preserved me in them," for his looking back to his former good life is only to bear witness to the providence of God.

29.1.5.en: * (The Apostle Paul) wants to say that God is the spring and source of all good things, and has no need of a partner or counselor. He is the beginning, the foundation and the maker of all good things; He is the Creator. He called that which did not exist into being. He governs all things, arranges them and keeps them according to His will!

29.2.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness" [3].

29.2.1.en: The light that shone from him was the light of God, who lit his lamp upon his head, as though Job were a lighthouse, worth nothing without the divine lamp. He owes everything to God, "the true Light," who led him through the darkness, gave him divine comforts in the midst of sorrows, and kept him from stumbling.

29.2.2.en: In a spirit of humility and with thanksgiving to God, Job presents himself as a lighthouse: whatever its metal, and whatever its shape, the secret of its power is the light placed at its summit, by which ships are guided from many miles away. Job confesses that even if he is a lighthouse, the light upon his head is the light of God and not his own. It is the lamp of the Lord, the true light.

29.2.3.en: The prophet David sees in the word of God "a lamp unto my feet" (Ps 119:105) that shines for him, so that he walks through the darkness of this world, but Job sees in the word of God a divine light fixed, as it were, upon his head to lead many ships toward the harbor!

29.2.4.en: It is fitting for the believer to bow before God, that He may fill his life with the work of His Holy Spirit, the Giver of enlightenment, and so he sings, saying, "In thy light shall we see light" (Ps 36:9). He did not say "I see," but "we see," for when the believer is enlightened he draws many with him to enjoy the divine light.

29.2.5.en: * When Job explained the goodness of his works, he added: "When his candle shined upon my head" (Job 29:3). This lamp is lit with the oil of good works for each one of us. But if we practice evil, and our works become evil, we not only fail to shine, but we also put out the lamp that is ours, and the saying of Scripture is fulfilled: "He that doeth evil walketh in darkness, and he that hateth his brother is in darkness" (see 1 Jn 2:11). Does it not appear to you that whoever extinguishes the light of love has extinguished the lamp? But whoever loves his brother (see 1 Jn 4:21) abides in the light of love, and can say with assurance: "But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God" (Ps 52:8), "thy children like olive plants round about thy table" (Ps 128:3).

29.2.6.en: Origen * "By the expression [candle] he means the light of Holy Scripture, of which (the Apostle Peter) says: 'We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts' (2 Pet 1:19). And the Psalmist says, 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Ps 119:105). Now because the upper part is the mind, and the mind is rightly called the head, it was said by the Psalmist: 'Thou anointest my head with oil' (Ps 23:5), as if he were saying plainly: You fill my soul with the fatness of love. Now the lamp shines upon the head of the Church, where the holy commandments enlighten the darkness of our minds, for in the darkness of this present life we receive the light of the word of God.

29.2.8.en: * Scripture enlightens the eyes of the soul, so read it, O wise one, and be filled with love for it. For from the reading of the Holy Scriptures the sun rises upon the minds that feed on them with discernment.

29.2.9.en: God placed the Holy Scriptures in the world as a lamp of light to illuminate its darkness. He who loves his soul is enlightened by reading, and walks by its guidance.

29.2.10.en: Approach Scripture with love, and contemplate its beauty. For you will not benefit without love, because love is the entrance to understanding.

29.2.11.en: Scripture demands your love; if you do not love it, do not read it.

29.2.12.en: It speaks to you, and if you grow weary of reading it, it deprives you of its hints.

29.2.13.en: You must love it, open it, read it and contemplate its beauty; otherwise do not read it, for if you do not love it you will not benefit from it.

29.3.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "As I was in the days of my autumn, when the favour of God was upon my tabernacle" [4].

29.3.1.en: The text came as it appears in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great): "And God sat with me in my tent." This phrase reveals God's surpassing humility and His wondrous love for man! Perhaps it points to the Incarnation of the divine Word, who became as one in our tent when He took on humanity.

29.3.2.en: Job looked at the days of his youth and counted them the days of his autumn, in which he had sensed God's favor upon his tent. In other words, he realized that in his youth he did not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but entered, as it were, into friendship with God, and God found His delight in the tent of Job, meeting with him, caring for him and leading him until He brought him across to the eternal dwelling.

29.3.3.en: * "As I was in the days of my youth, and God sat with me in my tent" [2]... Whoever meditates in silence on the commandments of God, in him God dwells secretly in his tent.

29.3.5.en: Job did not say that he enjoyed the sweetness of life in the days of his youth when he sat with his wife and his small children, or when the great men visited him in his tent and honored him, but what he remembered was that God overshadowed his tent like a special, cherished son, and came down to his tent to sit with him. What a wonderful picture of a man of God, whose whole concern is God's favor upon him, and His love for him, and His condescension to sit with him, speak with him and listen to him!

29.3.6.en: If God made of Job a lighthouse bearing a flame of divine light to guide ships to the safe heavenly harbor, then on the other hand He made of his tent a second heaven. It is as though God delights to come down and sit with His beloved Job!

29.3.7.en: If we look at our bodies as tents in which souls dwell during their journey in this world, then God, the Creator of the body, will not be disgusted by them or despise them, for they are the work of His hands. He sanctifies our bodies with all their emotions, senses and energies, dwells in them, and guides them so that we may enjoy the eternal, immortal glories.

29.4.0.en: "When the Almighty was yet with me, when my servants were about me" [5].

29.4.1.en: In his youth Job felt the love of God, and this was the secret of his sufficiency and satisfaction. He felt as though he were in a heavenly palace, not occupied with wealth, nor prestige, nor authority, but with his servants everyone was in fellowship with God, the true Lord of the house.

29.4.2.en: * Why do you refuse to imitate the holy men and women of the Old Testament? Tell me! Especially you, mothers, think of Hannah as an example; look at what she did. She brought her only son Samuel to the temple when he was still a child!

29.4.3.en: Which of you does not want her son to be like Samuel, who is better than a king over the whole world ten thousand times over? You say: This is impossible! My son will not be as great as he! Why is it impossible? Because in truth you do not want it. Entrust him into the hands of the One who is able to make him great. And who is this? God! For Hannah entrusted Samuel into the hands of God.

29.4.4.en: The high priest Eli was not truly able to shape him, for he failed in shaping his own two sons. It was the mother's faith and zeal that made everything possible. He was her firstborn and only son. She did not know whether she would have another son besides him, and yet she never said, "I will wait until he grows up and tastes the pleasures of the world, at least in his youth." No, she rejected all such thoughts. She had one aim, how from the beginning she could consecrate the joy of her heart to God.

29.4.5.en: Be ashamed, O men, before the wisdom of this woman. She offered Samuel to God, and with the Lord she left him. By this her marriage was blessed all the more, because her first aim was spiritual things. She consecrated the firstborn of her womb to God, and afterward received many children. She saw Samuel honored even in this life.

29.4.6.en: If men return honor for honor, will not God return much more to the one who honors Him? He gives abundantly even to those who do not honor Him at all!

29.4.7.en: How long shall we remain thus as lumps of flesh? How long shall we cling to the earth? Let everything come second to our care for our children, so that we bring them up in "the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4).

29.5.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "When I washed my steps with milk, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil" [6].

29.5.1.en: God gave him everything in abundance, so that from the multitude of his flocks it seemed to him as if he washed his feet with milk, and from the abundance of the fruit of the olive trees it seemed as if the rocks around him overflowed with oil.

29.5.2.en: To what does the washing of a man's steps with milk or richness, and the rock's pouring out rivers of oil for him, point, if not to the believer's sense of inner satisfaction, so that he has streams of milk in which he washes his feet, and streams of oil, so that not only are the members of his soul anointed with a smear of oil, but he becomes as one whose soul is immersed and drawn into streams of holy oil? Here he points to the stone olive press, from which oil flows like a river. "Then will I make their waters deep, and cause their rivers to run like oil, saith the Lord God" (Ezek 32:14). In the song of Moses before his departure it is said: "And he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock" (Deut 32:13).

29.5.3.en: The Psalmist sings, saying: "The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing" (Ps 145:15-16).

29.5.4.en: Moreover, since Job points to the Church, in preaching the Gospel of Christ she offers the world abundance and inner satisfaction. It is the preaching of the Crucified One, rejected by the world, yet in Him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in Him are all the treasures of heaven!

29.5.5.en: * "When I washed my feet with butter" [6]... The feet are washed with butter when the holy preachers are filled with the richness of good works.

29.5.6.en: "And the rock poured me out rivers of oil" [6]. By the rock he means Christ, as the great preacher affirms: "And that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4). This rock now pours out rivers of oil, which the holy Church uses, for the Lord speaks in her, and presents the preaching with the inner oil.

29.5.8.en: * Do you not want to be satisfied? And how can that be?! The body longs to be satisfied, but hunger returns to it again after digestion; therefore the Lord Christ says: "Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again" (Jn 4:13).

29.5.9.en: Then let us hunger and thirst after righteousness, that we may be filled with it... Let our inner man hunger and thirst, so that he may have the food and drink that suit him. (The Lord) said: "I am the bread which came down from heaven" (Jn 6:41). This is the bread of the hungry!

29.5.10.en: Let us also long to drink as the thirsty, "for with thee is the fountain of life" (Ps 36:9).

29.5.11.en: The Spiritual Elder * Ah! I shall not be satisfied until Your glory is revealed before me!

29.5.12.en: Yes, my God. For You alone are able to restore to me my happy life.

29.5.13.en: To You I confess my misery, at the passing of the day in which I was drowned among the many vanities of the world, deprived of You, the sole object of my love. That day in which my fleshly longings were scattered among deceptive delights. And how many of these delights carry in their pleasure countless toils! These delights promised me many things, and yet they brought upon me nothing but poverty. I moved from one to another, hoping that one of them might satisfy my soul, but they were unable, for my soul still lived only in You!

29.5.14.en: Truly, in You is beauty, You who alone are everlasting, exalted, and perfect always!

29.5.15.en: Whoever follows Your footsteps will never go astray! Whoever reaches You is overtaken by no despair!

29.5.16.en: Whoever possesses You has all his desires satisfied! But how hideous is my misery! Woe is me, my God, for my heart inclines to flee from You, You who are the true riches and the true joy, in order to follow a world in which there is nothing but sorrow and pain.

29.6.0.en: 7 "When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street! 8 The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up. 9 The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. 10 The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth.

29.6.1.en: "When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street!" [7].

29.6.2.en: His surpassing happiness in his house did not distract him from caring for others, so he would go out to the gate of the city to preside over the court of justice, not out of love of greatness, but so that all might enjoy justice and the spirit of injustice be lifted from those who suffered.

29.6.3.en: * "When I went out to the gate of the city, and in the street they prepared a seat for me"... It was the custom among the ancients that the elders sat at the gates and judged the cases of those entering the city, so that the people in the city might be safe, and those who were in dispute were not allowed to enter it. Now, while we honor the historical interpretation, we recall that Job did all this for the sake of preserving justice.

29.7.0.en: "The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up" [8].

29.7.1.en: He had great awe, so that those who walked in immaturity, like reckless youths, feared him. These saw him and hid from him, lest their evils be exposed. But those who walked as experienced, wise elders stood in reverence and respect for him. As the Apostle says: "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour" (1 Tim 5:17). "Render therefore to all their dues... fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour" (Rom 13:7).

29.7.2.en: * "The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up" [8]. If we look to the historical interpretation, we believe what he says. If we take what he said in a symbolic sense, then those whose souls are not weighed down with the weight of counsels are called "young men." Holy Scripture usually calls those who have weight (experience from the past) in their characters elders, not only because they have become mature through the number of years... One of the wise says: "For honourable age is not that which standeth in length of time, nor that is measured by number of years. But wisdom is the gray hair unto men, and an unspotted life is old age" (Wis 4:8-9)...

29.7.3.en: Now [the young men see] the holy Church and hide, and the elders arise and stand, because the immature fear her activity and uprightness, while the elders glorify her. The trifling in thought flee, while the serious and the perfect praise her by rising to be worthy of her life. The imperfect blame her order and her perfect love. [The young men see her and hide], because they fear that their hidden conduct will be discovered.

29.8.0.en: "The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth" [9].

29.9.0.en: "The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth" [10].

29.9.1.en: Job had a strong personality founded on his wisdom, abilities and gifts, so he was the object of honor from the great and the noble. In his presence all fell silent to listen to him, and to benefit from his wisdom and his surpassing experience. Perhaps when the great and the noble quarreled over a matter or differed in opinion, they would find the decisive solution with Job.

29.9.2.en: * "The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. The voice of the rulers is hushed, and their tongue cleaveth to the roof of their mouth" [9-10]. Who are those understood here as leaders or nobles but those who spread heretical evils? Of these it is said by the Psalmist: "He poureth contempt upon princes, and causeth them to wander in the wilderness, where there is no way" (Ps 107:40). For such persons do not fear to interpret the dispensation of God in a wrong sense, and certainly they draw the flocks subject to them into a wilderness without a way, and not into the Way, which is Christ. Upon these contempt (strife) is rightly poured out, and then they are like those who lay their fingers on their mouths....

29.9.3.en: Their tongue cleaves to their mouth, since they do not dare to utter what is evil in unrestrained speech, but they cover over all that they do within themselves, lest they propose anything untrue against the true faith... "The voice of the rulers is hushed, and their tongue cleaveth to their mouth." It is as if the Church says plainly: When I am given the opportunity to preach in a loud, public voice, every man who is not subject to the truth is afraid of me.

29.9.5.en: To the extent that God gives His children honor, they fear falling into pride, so they work in a spirit of humility, but they do not lag behind in working with burning zeal. If their works appear, it is for the glory of God, and if they are hidden, it is for their preservation in the fortress of humility, full of safety.

29.9.6.en: * It is among the marks of the saints to hide the good works they have done, lest they bring upon themselves a fall into boasting. Therefore the Truth says: "Take heed that ye do not your righteousness before men, to be seen of them" (Mt 6:1). So also, when He gave sight to the two blind men sitting by the way, He commanded them, saying, "See that no man know it" (Mt 9:30). Yet it is said of them that they "departed, and spread abroad his fame in all that country"... It was fitting for them to hide for the sake of some purpose, and to make it known out of necessity.

29.9.7.en: Let their hiding be for the preservation of their souls, and let their making it known be for the benefit of others. For this reason it is written: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mt 5:15-16). There are times when saints are obliged to practice good works even in the presence of their fellow creatures, or to tell them what they are doing, but not with the aim that they themselves be glorified by these works, but that their Father who is in heaven be glorified...

29.9.8.en: For this reason good preachers avoid honor, and yet they wish to be honored so that others may imitate them.

29.9.9.en: In the same way, certainly, when the Apostle Paul spoke with his disciples he fled from honor, and yet he shows how much he deserves to be greatly honored. For he said to the Thessalonians: "Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ, but we were gentle among you" (1 Thess 2:6-7). Again, in his epistle to the Corinthians, avoiding honor, he says: "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord" (2 Cor 4:5)... Therefore he showed in a marvelous way the grace of humility, and sought an abundance of benefit, as one who declares himself the servant of his disciples, and proves that he is better than his enemies.

29.10.0.en: 11 "When the ear heard me, then it blessed me; and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me: 12 Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him. 13 The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy. 14 I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem. 15 I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame. 16 I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out. 17 And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth.

29.10.1.en: "When the ear heard me, then it blessed me;

29.10.2.en: and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me" [11].

29.10.3.en: This honor did not rest on his wealth, nor on his authority, but on his practical conduct, for all bore witness to him through the ear's hearing of his wisdom and his judgments, and the eye's seeing of his love and tenderness. He imitated the just God, the Lover of mankind, and so all bore witness to him.

29.10.4.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in the person of the blessed Job a symbol of the blessed Church, for the Church has her esteem, honor and blessing from all who listen to her and see her holy life. The Church remains persecuted by her opponents, but she is blessed, awesome and honored.

29.11.0.en: "Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him" [12].

29.11.1.en: The blessing of all upon him rested on his works of love, for he would not rest until the poor man found his rest, and no food pleased him until the orphan found help in him.

29.11.2.en: St. Basil the Great asks us to imitate righteous Job, who became a father to orphans and a helper to them (Job 29:12). He presented a deep spiritual understanding of this fatherly work. The adoption of orphans does not stop at supporting them materially, but extends to embracing the little ones in order to consecrate their hearts and lives to the Lord. In his answer to the question: "At what age is a person permitted to dedicate himself to God, and at what time is the vow of virginity considered safe?" he answers thus: [Since the Lord says, "Suffer the little children to come unto me" (Mk 10:14), and the Apostle commends the one who knows Holy Scripture from childhood (2 Tim 3:15), and the one who directs his children to be brought up "in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4), it seems to us that all times of life, even the very early, are suitable for acceptance into discipleship (monasticism). Truly we must receive those children who are deprived of their parents under our care, and so become fathers to the orphans, imitating Job (Job 29:12).]

29.11.3.en: * To make clear why they declare him blessed, he cites his good works, saying: [Because I delivered the one who cried from the hand of those who oppressed him], but this comes after he first ascribes the merit to God, who kept and preserved him, so that "he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord" (1 Cor 1:31).

29.11.4.en: * See, he does not boast that he turned aside from evil, nor that he offered sacrifices as the Jews did, but boasts that he fulfills what God wants (the rescue of the poor). He says: "Judge the fatherless, plead for the widow" (Isa 1:17). Note that he does not abuse his authority, but uses it when there is a need for it. He was a father and a defender to all. He did not use his riches for injustice, nor his glory for boasting, nor his wisdom for evil, but to rescue those who were weighed down by the pressure of the wicked.

29.11.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Now the holy Church shows these works of tenderness on the material side, and does not cease to show them spiritually. She rescues the poor man who cries out when she forgives the sins that the sinner commits and he asks forgiveness for them. Of this poor man it is said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3). The cry of such poor is the cry of those who say with the voice of the Psalmist: "Let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low" (Ps 79:8).

29.11.6.en: Now she rescues [the fatherless who has none to help him], when each one flees from the desires of the persecuting world... and runs to the bosom of the holy Church, and finds in her the help of counsel. Perhaps by "the fatherless" is meant any believer who, through the death of the good father, becomes an orphan, deprived of him for a time, but not deprived of consolation.

29.12.0.en: "The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy" [13].

29.12.1.en: Those under destructive pressures found their rescue in him and were saved, and their blessing came upon him, for they did not cease to pray for him, and the broken hearts of widows were gladdened and rejoiced at his works of love and tenderness.

29.12.2.en: If God attributes to Himself the despised, the needy and the broken-hearted, as the Father of the fatherless and the Judge of the widows, then Job found his delight in caring for all these suffering groups.

29.12.3.en: * How highly the holy Job esteemed the dignity of death, when he said: [May the blessing of him who drew near to death come upon me] (Job 29:13)... If we see any poor person at the moment of death, let us help him at our own expense. Let each person say: [May the blessing of the person who was near death come upon me]. If we see anyone in weakness, let us not abandon him. If we see anyone in his last sufferings, let us not leave him... May everyone, as he dies, praise you; everyone who dies of old age or of a serious wound or suffering from illness, at the moment of death. This saying has brought blessing to very many... May the last words a person utters before his death be to repeat your name, and as his soul departs from his body, may his blessing come upon you.

29.12.4.en: * If it is our duty to show mercy to all, should we not rather show it to that good man (the believer who is suffering imprisonment)?! And if he receives nothing from you at the time of danger when he is being led to death, and you think that your money is better than the life of the man who is dying, what a sin you commit! Therefore Job says his wonderful saying: [May the blessing of him who is on the way to destruction and death come upon me] (Job 29:13).

29.12.5.en: St. Ambrose * And "the blessing of him that was ready to perish" came upon her (that is, upon the Church, who cares for his salvation), when she anticipates the perishing of the sinner, and by her holy counsels turns him back from the pit of sin. It is written thus: "He which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins" (Jas 5:20). It is a matter deserving great reward to be saved from the death of the body, which will die sooner or later; how much more does he deserve who frees a soul from death, to live in the heavenly city without end?

29.12.7.en: "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me:

29.13.0.en: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem" [14].

29.13.1.en: His tender conduct, in that he did not allow anyone to be wronged or insulted, nor a needy person to be humiliated, was not a certain role he was bound to play, but was his garment that he never took off. He counted these works not a secondary matter in his life, but a necessity, without which he would be stripped bare before God Himself, and would return to the state of his parents Adam and Eve, sheltering under the fig tree in fear and trembling, with nakedness and shame!

29.13.2.en: He counted the works of righteousness not a gift from himself that he bestows on others, but a divine gift that clothes him with glory. It is a royal turban (crown)! He did not wear the crown of kingship for boasting and honor; rather his crown was justice and mercy. His honor was not in the royal purple robe, nor the crown, nor the scepter, but his honor and warmth were in the garment of righteousness and the crown of truth.

29.13.3.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that Job put on righteousness like a cloak, or like one who puts on the garment of a judge. No one appointed him judge over the people, but his virtuous, holy life impelled him to this work, and made the people willingly accept his judgment in their cases. Just as the virtuous life of Moses prepared him for the work of leadership, so for Job, his practice of judicial work came naturally from his virtuous life.

29.13.4.en: * He says, "I put on righteousness," for there are persons who have a greater standing than others, but they often practice injustice. This was not the case with Job, for he lived always in the way of righteousness.

29.13.5.en: [I put on righteousness like a cloak], that is, it is my garment for adornment. Some are displeased with this work, murmur, and feel that it is wearisome and hard, but I am not so... And yet who appointed him as judge? This came from his own person, because of his virtue, as with Moses. This is how men ought to be. But as for him who denies virtue, governors are set over him.

29.13.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * We are obliged to condemn ourselves, so that even when the matter is against us it turns to our favor, as we become accusers of ourselves and condemn our sins. And Scripture says: [The righteous is first in his own cause] (see Prov 18:17). And again he says: "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me as a robe" (Job 29:14). Our present garment is usually, without doubt, an armor for war rather than a garment of peace, as long as we are still subject to desire; but it is different when our last enemy is scattered, and righteousness is full and complete, with no enemy to harass us.

29.13.7.en: St. Augustine * The man who wanted to harm Jacob was not able to send him away empty (Gen 31:29). For the wise person will never be empty, but always wears the garment of prudence, and is able to say, as Job said: [I clothe myself with righteousness, and put on justice] (Job 29:14). Truly this is the inner tunic of the spirit, and no one can strip it from him unless the man himself takes it off by his erring conduct. Truly Adam was found naked and stripped (Gen 3:10-11), while Joseph was not found naked even when his outer garment was taken from him, since he was wrapped in the safe garment of virtue. For this reason the wise man will not be found empty. How could he be empty? His soul is in fullness, being guarded in the garments it has received.

29.13.8.en: St. Ambrose * The way to wisdom is not like a man coming out of water into the air, who at the moment he rises above the surface of the water suddenly breathes freely, but like a man coming out of darkness into light, upon whom the light dawns gradually as he advances. So as long as this is not fully achieved, we speak of man as one who enjoys the light gradually. As he approaches the mouth of the cave, whatever light he has comes from the light into which he is advancing, and whatever darkness remains in him comes from the darkness he is leaving. For this reason it is rightly said that in the sight of God "shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). And yet "the just shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4); so on one side the saints put on righteousness, and on the other side no one lives wholly without sin. Some sin much and others less, and the best of men is he who sins very little.

29.13.9.en: St. Augustine * [I put on righteousness, and it was my clothing] [14]. Certainly when we put on a garment we are surrounded on every side. In the same way, he who clothes himself with righteousness as with a garment defends himself on every side by good practice, and leaves no part of his conduct bare to sin. For whoever is righteous in some works and unjust in others is like one who has covered one side and left the other side naked. Good works that are afterward defiled by evil deeds do not produce good. It is said by Solomon: "He that offendeth in one thing destroyeth much good" (Eccl 9:18) (Vulgate). And James says: "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all" (Jas 2:10). And he carefully explained this saying by adding: "For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law" (a).

29.13.10.en: Thus we look with the eyes of the heart in every direction, and so we are careful with all diligence on every side. Therefore it is rightly said also by Solomon: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Prov 4:23). Before "diligence" he first added "all." Certainly it is fitting for everyone to examine himself diligently from this side and that. And as long as he is in this life he knows that he is set in a battle in which he fights against spiritual enemies, lest he lose the reward which he obtains through one set of works by another. Lest on one side he shut the door in the face of the enemy, but open a door to him on another side. For if a city has great protective barricades against deceiving enemies, and is fortified with strong walls, and is guarded on every side by sleepless watchmen, but a single unfortified opening is found through negligence, the enemy will certainly enter...

29.13.11.en: Take that Pharisee who went up into the temple to pray; let us hear how he had fortifications for the city of himself, for he says: "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess." He who says, "I thank thee," certainly set up extraordinary fortifications. But let us see where he left an undefended opening toward the plans of the enemy. ["I am not as this publican"] (Lk 18:11-12). Behold, you see how he opened the city of his heart to the plans of the enemy through his praise of himself, the city which he had closed up in vain with fasting and almsgiving.

29.14.0.en: "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" [15].

29.14.1.en: God granted him to be eyes to the blind, offering good counsel to those who were perplexed. And he was feet to the lame, for it did not stop at giving advice, but in love he undertook everything to be feet that lead the lame in the way of truth, bringing them in practice to the life of rejoicing in the Lord.

29.14.2.en: * "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" [15]. He did not say, "I lightened their sorrows," nor "I hid from them their sense of blindness," but [I was their eyes]... In every place I turned their darkness into light.

29.14.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * By saying these things he indicated unmistakably that he stretched out his hand to one, and carried the other...

29.14.4.en: * By preaching the Church enlightens the blind, while she supports the lame with her help. For the blind man is the one who does not see where he is going, and the lame man is the one who has no ability to go to the place he sees. Sin is often committed either through ignorance (blindness) or weakness (lameness); either a man does not know what he ought to desire, or he is not able to do all that he desires.

29.15.0.en: "I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out" [16].

29.15.1.en: He was not only a defender of the poor and generous toward them, but offered a sincere fatherhood, for though a king he did not disdain to call himself a father to the poor.

29.15.2.en: If a case was brought to him he did not hasten to judge, but took care to listen to all the parties and to examine all sides precisely, for he would not answer a matter before he heard it (Prov 18:13), nor issue judgment at first glance merely on appearance. "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Prov 18:17).

29.15.3.en: Through Job's tender fatherhood he cared not only for the one who asked him to rescue him from injustice, but also for the one who did not ask him. He found his delight in searching for broken souls to rescue them, so he examined the causes that had not been presented to him nor known by him.

29.15.4.en: Someone may ask: If we wish to show some kind of tenderness or fatherhood toward others, should we care for their bodily affairs, when the Lord Christ asked the one He called to work with Him to let the dead bury their dead, and to devote himself to spiritual service (Lk 9:60)? Pope Gregory (the Great) answers this question, saying: [Above all, those who shine with spiritual gifts must not entirely ignore the affairs of their weak brethren, but they should entrust this matter to others, so that one suited to it may manage it.]

29.15.5.en: * Truly, blessed is he who does not send the poor man away from his house empty-handed. There is none more blessed than he who feels the needs of the poor and the distress of the weak and helpless. For on the day of judgment he receives salvation from the Lord, who counts Himself a debtor to him for the works of mercy he has shown.

29.15.6.en: St. Ambrose * "And the cause which I knew not I searched out" [16]. Look, for his role as an advocate (rescuer) does not consist in giving money only, or food or clothing, but extends to preserving them from dangers as well. In a battle that is not mine I take the front position. In the matter that concerns me I search like a skilled hunter. It is not in the things known to me... I refused to abandon them as some do today, and not only do I not refuse those who are present, but even if there is no one seeking him I seek him out myself, as though my work were digging. So I work continually to observe with all care whether anyone has been oppressed.

29.15.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * But if anyone wants to learn how we call God "Father," let him listen to Moses, the excellent teacher, when he says: ["Is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?"] (Deut 32:6). And the prophet Isaiah also says: "But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay... and we all are the work of thy hand" (Isa 64:8). The prophetic gift has declared most clearly that we call Him Father not according to nature, but by the work of God's grace in adoption.

29.15.8.en: And so that you may learn more precisely from the divine Holy Scripture that not only is he who is a natural father called "father," but others also, hear what the Apostle says: ["For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel"] (1 Cor 4:15). Paul was a father to the Corinthians, not because he begot them according to the flesh but through teaching, and he begot them again according to the Spirit.

29.15.9.en: Hear also Job: "I was a father to the poor." He called himself a father, not because he begot them all, but because of his care for them.

29.16.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem "And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth" [17].

29.16.1.en: As much as he offered tender fatherhood to the poor, he did not fear the violence of the wicked, unjust and proud. "I brake the jaws of the wicked." He did not say that he takes revenge on them or kills them, but he shatters the powers of evil and violence, and takes the prey from between their teeth, and delivers it with courage, as David rescued the lamb from the mouth of the lion.

29.16.2.en: * "I brake the jaws of the wicked." This is what the Apostle commands: ["He that ruleth, with diligence"] (see Rom 12:8).

29.16.3.en: "And plucked the spoil out of his teeth." Note the difficulty of the work. Those who have already been preyed upon and seized, he sets their affairs right... Note also that his virtue is incomparable in every case. If the situation called for it he punished, and if the situation called for it he supported others.

29.16.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * See what prey the Church snatches from the mouth of Satan, for she took Saul the plunderer at his conversion! While he was still breathing out threatenings on his way to Damascus with letters to persecute the believers, he was gathering prey for Satan, but he himself was gathered for Christ's account when he received the faith (Acts 9:1-19). The Church often snatches the prey from the mouth of the wicked one, and often rescues the soul from the grip of error by preaching...

29.16.5.en: By the jaws the hidden plans (of the devil) are shown, and by the teeth the open practice of sin is shown. The Psalmist said of these jaws and teeth: "Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O Lord" (Ps 58:6).
